title: 资源分配与阶段检查 · Three academic readings
instructions: 原创模拟训练材料；先独立作答，再核对依据。三篇文章共40题，限时60分钟。
passage:
Passage 1: The Community Garden Project: Planning, Checking, and Sharing Resources

In the small town of Greenfield, a group of residents decided to turn an unused piece of land into a community garden. The land had stood empty for several years, and the residents believed it could be put to much better use. The project, called the Greenfield Community Garden, aimed to provide fresh vegetables for local families and to create a pleasant space for neighbours to meet. From the beginning, the idea attracted a great deal of interest, and many people offered to help. However, the project faced a major challenge: how to share limited resources fairly among many eager volunteers. With so many people wanting to take part, the organisers knew that clear rules would be essential if the garden was to succeed.

The first task was to divide the land into plots. The organisers measured the area carefully and found that they could create twenty plots of equal size. Each plot would be about 20 square metres, which was enough space for a family to grow a useful amount of vegetables. They also had a limited water supply: only one tap for the whole garden. If every gardener used water without thinking, the tap would run dry quickly. Therefore, the group agreed on a rule: each plot could use water for only 30 minutes per day, and watering was allowed only in the early morning or late evening to reduce evaporation. These simple rules helped ensure that everyone had enough water throughout the growing season.

Seeds and tools were another issue. A local shop donated 100 packets of seeds, including tomatoes, carrots, and beans. The organisers decided that each gardener could take five packets, but they had to return empty packets to show they had used them. This helped track how many seeds were left and prevented waste. Tools were more difficult: there were only ten spades and five watering cans for twenty plots. So the group set up a sharing system. Gardeners signed up for tool use on a noticeboard, and each person could borrow a spade for two hours at a time. This system worked well because most people only needed tools for short periods, and the noticeboard made it easy to see when tools were free.

As the weeks passed, the organisers realised they needed to check progress regularly. They introduced a monthly meeting where gardeners could discuss problems and share tips. At the first meeting, one gardener, Mrs. Chen, said that her tomatoes were not growing well. Another gardener, Mr. Patel, suggested that she might be watering too much. After checking, they found that Mrs. Chen's plot received water from a leaking pipe, so the soil was too wet. The group fixed the pipe and Mrs. Chen's tomatoes improved. This showed the value of regular checks and of gardeners helping one another.

The project also had to manage money. The town council gave them a small grant of £500. The organisers used £200 for seeds and tools, £150 for a new water tank, and £100 for a fence to keep animals out. The remaining £50 was kept for emergencies. They recorded every purchase in a notebook, and at each monthly meeting, they reviewed the spending. This transparency helped everyone trust the organisers and understand how the money was being used.

Not everything went smoothly. Some gardeners felt that the tool-sharing system was unfair because people with more free time could borrow tools more often. To solve this, the group introduced a rule that each person could borrow tools for a maximum of four hours per week. This ensured that everyone had a fair chance. They also started a buddy system, where experienced gardeners helped newcomers. This not only improved skills but also built friendships among the volunteers.

By the end of the first season, the garden had produced over 200 kilograms of vegetables. The organisers held a harvest festival to celebrate. They invited all volunteers and their families. At the festival, they asked for feedback. Many people said they enjoyed the project but suggested that next year they should plant more fruit trees. Others wanted more benches for resting. The organisers wrote down all suggestions and promised to consider them for the next season.

In conclusion, the Greenfield Community Garden project shows how careful planning and regular checking can help a community share limited resources effectively. By setting clear rules, monitoring progress, and listening to feedback, the group turned a small piece of land into a valuable asset for the whole town.

Passage 2: The Community Garden Project: Planning, Planting, and Checking Progress

Last spring, the residents of Maple Street decided to turn an unused piece of land into a community garden. The idea came from a neighborhood meeting where several people said they wanted a shared space for growing food and spending time outdoors. The project was small but ambitious. They had a budget of $2,000, a group of 15 volunteers, and only three months before the summer festival, when they hoped to show the garden to the wider community. The first task was to allocate resources wisely, because the budget was limited and every dollar had to count. The group leader, Maria, suggested spending 40% of the budget on seeds and plants, 30% on tools and equipment, and the remaining 30% on water and soil improvements. Some members disagreed. They wanted to spend more on a decorative fence. After a long discussion, the group agreed to follow Maria's plan but to use recycled materials for the fence. This compromise saved money and kept everyone happy, and it set a positive tone for the rest of the project.

Once the budget was set, the volunteers began preparing the land. They cleared weeds, tested the soil, and built eight raised beds. Each bed was assigned to a small team of two or three people. The teams were responsible for planting, watering, and weeding their own beds. However, they also had to help with shared areas like the paths and the compost bin, so everyone understood that the garden depended on cooperation. To track progress, Maria created a simple chart on the garden shed wall. Every week, each team marked what they had done and what they still needed. This visual record helped everyone see how the project was developing. For example, in the first month, the teams planted tomatoes, beans, and lettuce. By the second month, the beans were growing well, but the tomatoes needed more support. The chart showed that the tomato team needed extra stakes, so they borrowed some from a neighboring garden.

At the end of each month, the group held a review meeting. They discussed what had worked and what had not. In the first review, they realized they had used too much water. The soil was not holding moisture well. They decided to add compost to improve the soil. This was an extra cost, but they took it from the tool budget, which had some leftover money. In the second review, they noticed that some volunteers were not coming regularly. Instead of blaming them, the group asked for feedback. They learned that evening work was difficult for people with families. So they changed the schedule to include more weekend sessions. This adjustment increased volunteer attendance by 50%. The reviews also helped them plan for the future. They decided to save 10% of the remaining budget for next year's seeds.

The project was not without challenges. A heatwave in July dried out some of the plants. The group had to buy extra water, which they had not planned for. They used the contingency fund they had set aside at the beginning. This fund was 5% of the total budget. Because they had planned for emergencies, the garden survived. By the end of the summer, they had harvested over 50 kilograms of vegetables. They shared the produce among the volunteers and donated some to a local food bank. The project was considered a success, not just because of the harvest, but because of the teamwork and the lessons learned. Maria said, "We didn't just grow vegetables; we grew a community."

Looking back, the group identified three key factors for their success. First, they had a clear budget plan that everyone understood. Second, they checked their progress regularly and adjusted their actions when needed. Third, they communicated openly and solved problems together. These factors are now part of a guide that the group has written for other neighborhoods. The guide includes templates for budget charts, progress trackers, and review meeting agendas. It also suggests starting small and being flexible. The Maple Street garden is now in its second year, and the group is using the same approach. They have expanded to 12 raised beds and have a waiting list of volunteers. The project shows that with careful planning and regular checks, even a small community can achieve a lot. In addition, the group has learned that sharing tasks and listening to each other are just as important as money and tools. They hope other neighborhoods will use their guide and avoid some of the same mistakes. The garden has also become a place where neighbors meet and support each other, which makes the whole community stronger.

Passage 3: The Community Garden: Planning for a Shared Harvest

In the small town of Greenfield, a group of residents decided to turn an unused piece of land into a community garden. The idea came from a public meeting, where several neighbours said they wanted a safe and friendly place to grow vegetables and spend time outdoors. The garden was divided into 20 equal plots, and each household that joined received one plot. However, not all plots were the same: some had better soil, and some received more sunlight. To make things fair, the garden committee decided that each household would pay a small fee based on the size of its plot, and the money would be used to buy shared tools and seeds. The committee also agreed that every household must contribute two hours of work each month to maintain the common areas, such as the paths and the water tank. These rules were written down and signed by every household at the start, so everyone knew what was expected. Clear written rules helped people understand their duties and reduced confusion later.

After three months, the committee did a stage check to see how well the plan was working. They found that some households were not doing their two hours of work. For example, the Chen family, who had a plot near the entrance, had done only three hours in total instead of six. When asked, Mrs. Chen explained that her husband had been ill and she had to take care of him. The committee decided to be flexible: they allowed the Chen family to do extra hours in the next month. However, they also noticed that the Lee family, who had a plot with the best soil, had not paid the fee for two months. Mr. Lee said he thought the fee was too high. The committee reminded him that the fee was agreed by everyone at the start, and if he did not pay, the shared tools could not be bought. Finally, Mr. Lee paid the fee. The committee was pleased that both problems were solved through talking rather than punishment. This showed that listening to people's reasons can solve problems in a peaceful way.

Another issue was water. The garden had one water tank, which was filled once a week. In the first month, some households used too much water, and the tank was empty by the weekend. This meant that other households had no water for their plants. The committee then set a rule: each plot could use only 50 liters of water per week. They also asked households to water their plants in the early morning or late evening to reduce evaporation. After this change, the water lasted the whole week. The committee also checked the tools: two spades were broken, and the wheelbarrow had a flat tire. They used some of the fee money to repair them. These small repairs cost less than buying new tools, so the shared money was used wisely. Fixing things quickly also meant that work in the garden could continue without long delays.

At the end of the sixth month, the committee did another stage check. They found that most households were now following the rules. The average work hours per household had increased from 1.5 hours per month to 2.2 hours per month. Water usage had dropped by 30%. The committee decided to continue the garden for another year. They also planned to add a small shed for storing tools, using the remaining fee money. Mrs. Chen, whose husband had recovered, volunteered to organize a monthly gardening workshop. In the workshop, families could learn how to grow vegetables and how to use water carefully. The committee agreed that the garden had become a good example of how a community can share resources fairly. The workshops also gave families a chance to meet and help each other.

However, not everything was perfect. The committee noted that the plot with the best soil, which belonged to the Lee family, produced more vegetables than other plots. Some other households felt this was unfair. The committee explained that the soil quality was natural and could not be changed easily. They suggested that the Lee family share some of their extra vegetables with others, and the Lee family agreed. The committee also decided that in the future, they would rotate the plots every two years so that everyone would have a chance to use the better soil. This decision was welcomed by all. The committee felt that fairness was not only about rules, but also about listening and finding solutions that everyone could accept.

grammar.title: 条件句；数量词；段落间的指代与衔接
grammar.explanation: 条件句用来表达“如果……就……”：真实条件句用if+一般现在时，主句用一般将来时（will+动词原形）。数量词如some, many, a few, a little, enough等用来表示不确定的数量。段落之间常用代词（如this, they, it）和连接词（如however, therefore, also）来指代前文内容并使文章连贯。
grammar.example: If every gardener used water without thinking, the tap would run dry quickly.

questions.prompt: If it ______ tomorrow, we will cancel the garden meeting.
questions.explanation: 真实条件句中，if从句用一般现在时表示将来，主句用will+动词原形。因此选rains。
questions.evidence: If every gardener used water without thinking, the tap would run dry quickly.

questions.explanation: volunteers是可数名词复数，比较级用fewer。less用于不可数名词。
questions.evidence: there were only ten spades and five watering cans for twenty plots.

questions.prompt: The organisers bought a new water tank. ______, they fixed the leaking pipe.
questions.explanation: 这里表示并列或补充关系，用Also。However表示转折，Therefore表示结果，For example表示举例。
questions.evidence: They also started a buddy system, where experienced gardeners helped newcomers.

questions.prompt: Mrs. Chen’s tomatoes were not growing well. ______, the group checked her plot and found a leaking pipe.
questions.explanation: 前后是因果关系，因此用As a result（结果）。
questions.evidence: After checking, they found that Mrs. Chen’s plot received water from a leaking pipe, so the soil was too wet.
